topics.title: Types of Operating Systems
topics.definition: Operating systems are classified by how they manage jobs, users and time constraints.

children.title: Batch operating system
children.definition: Jobs with similar needs are grouped and run without user interaction, which wastes time while waiting for I/O.

children.title: Multiprogramming system
children.definition: Several jobs stay in memory so the CPU can switch to another job while one waits for I/O.

children.title: Time sharing (multitasking) system
children.definition: The CPU switches rapidly among interactive users, giving each a small time slice.

children.title: Real time system
children.definition: Hard and soft real time systems must meet deadlines, used in control and embedded applications.

children.title: Distributed and network operating systems
children.definition: Distributed systems present many machines as one, while network systems let users log in to separate machines.

children.title: Embedded and mobile operating systems
children.definition: Small footprint systems for appliances, phones such as Android, and IoT devices.

card.explanation: Operating systems are grouped by how they handle jobs, users and deadlines. A batch system collects similar jobs and runs them with no interaction, which leaves the processor idle during input and output. Multiprogramming keeps several jobs in memory so the processor switches to another while one waits, which raises utilisation. Time sharing switches fast enough that each user feels they have the machine, which is what interactive terminals needed. Real time systems must meet deadlines, hard ones strictly and soft ones usually. Distributed systems present many machines as one, while embedded and mobile systems fit into phones and appliances.
card.example: A college exam result job that runs overnight with no one watching is batch work. The lab terminals that must answer every keystroke at once are time sharing.

quiz.q: Which system keeps several jobs in memory so the CPU switches while one waits for I/O?
quiz.why: Keeping more than one job ready is what stops the processor idling during input and output.

quiz.q: Which system must meet strict deadlines?
quiz.why: Hard real time systems must never miss a deadline, as in aircraft or medical control.

quiz.q: Which statement about OS types is NOT correct?
options: Batch systems run without user interaction
Time sharing gives each user a slice of time
Multiprogramming keeps only one job in memory at a time
Distributed systems present many machines as one
quiz.why: Holding several jobs in memory at once is the whole point of multiprogramming.

quiz.q: Android is an example of which kind of operating system?
quiz.why: Android is built for phones, which means a small footprint and tight power limits.

quiz.q: What is the difference between hard and soft real time?
options: Hard real time must never miss a deadline, soft may occasionally
Soft real time is used in aircraft
quiz.why: Missing a hard deadline is a system failure, while missing a soft one only degrades quality.

card.examTip: List the six types with one line each, and underline the difference between multiprogramming and time sharing.

topics.title: Operating System Structures
topics.definition: The structure of an operating system describes how its components are organised and how they communicate.

children.title: Simple or monolithic structure
children.definition: One large kernel in which any procedure can call any other, as in early MS-DOS and UNIX.

children.title: Layered structure
children.definition: The system is divided into levels, each using only the level below, which is easier to debug but slower.

children.title: Microkernel structure
children.definition: Only essential services stay in the kernel while others run as user processes, improving reliability and security.

children.title: Modular and hybrid structure
children.definition: Loadable kernel modules combine flexibility with speed; hybrid kernels mix monolithic and microkernel ideas.

children.title: Virtual machine structure
children.definition: A layer of software presents several virtual copies of the hardware to different operating systems.

card.explanation: Structure is how the pieces of an operating system are arranged. A monolithic kernel is one large program in which any procedure can call any other, which is fast but hard to maintain. A layered system is built in levels, each using only the level below, which is easier to debug and slower in practice. A microkernel keeps only the essentials in the kernel and runs the rest as user processes. That improves reliability, because a failed service can be restarted. Modular and hybrid designs load parts of the kernel at run time, and a virtual machine layer offers several copies of the hardware.
card.example: Linux is monolithic but modular, so drivers can be loaded while it runs. A microkernel system runs the file system and the drivers outside the kernel as ordinary processes.

quiz.q: Which structure keeps only essential services in the kernel?
quiz.why: Everything else runs as a user process, so a crash there does not bring down the kernel.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of a layered structure?
options: It is easier to debug and verify
quiz.why: Each level uses only the one below, so a fault can usually be traced to one layer.

quiz.q: Which statement about structures is NOT correct?
options: A monolithic kernel is fast but hard to maintain
Loadable modules let a kernel grow at run time
A monolithic kernel cannot support device drivers
quiz.why: Monolithic kernels hold the drivers inside the kernel, which is why they are large.

quiz.q: What does a virtual machine structure present to the guest?
options: A copy of the source code
quiz.why: Each guest operating system believes it owns the machine, which is the point of the layer.

quiz.q: Why is a microkernel considered more secure?
options: Fewer services run with full privilege, so the trusted core is smaller
It is written in a safer language
It has more lines of code
quiz.why: A smaller privileged core means less code that could damage the whole system.

card.examTip: Draw the four structures in a row and write one advantage and one disadvantage under each.

topics.title: System Components and Operating System Services
topics.definition: The main components manage processes, memory, files, I/O, storage, protection and networking, and the services are what users and programs need.

children.title: Process management
children.definition: Creating, scheduling, synchronising and terminating processes and threads.

children.title: Memory management
children.definition: Tracking memory use, allocating and freeing space, and managing virtual memory.

children.title: File and storage management
children.definition: Creating, organising and protecting files, directories and secondary storage.

children.title: I/O and networking management
children.definition: Device drivers, buffering, caching and spooling for input output, plus protocols for communication.

children.title: Protection and security
children.definition: Controlling access to resources and defending against internal and external attacks.

children.title: User services versus system services
children.definition: User interfaces, program execution, I/O and file operations versus resource allocation, accounting and error detection.

card.explanation: An operating system is best understood by the components it holds. Process management creates, schedules, synchronises and terminates processes and threads. Memory management tracks what memory is used, allocates and frees it and runs virtual memory. File and storage management organises files and directories on disk and decides who may reach them. Input output is handled through device drivers with buffering, caching and spooling, and networking adds the protocols. Protection and security run across all of them, controlling who may use what.
card.example: Printing a project report uses spooling. The file is queued to disk so the program finishes at once, and the printer takes it at its own pace.

quiz.q: Which component decides which process runs on the CPU next?
quiz.why: Creating, scheduling and terminating processes and threads is the process manager's work.

quiz.q: What is spooling used for?
options: Holding output for a slow device such as a printer
quiz.why: The queue on disk frees the program at once instead of making it wait for the device.

quiz.q: Which statement about components is NOT correct?
options: Networking is handled entirely by the application layer
Device drivers are part of I/O management
quiz.why: The operating system implements the protocol stack, and applications reach it through sockets.

quiz.q: Which of these is a user service rather than a system service?
quiz.why: Program execution, I/O and file operations are offered to users; allocation and accounting run behind them.

quiz.q: Which component decides who may read a file?
quiz.why: Access control is a protection duty, and it applies to files, memory and devices alike.

card.examTip: List the six components with one duty each, then split the services into the user and system groups.

topics.title: System Calls, System Programs and Operating System Design
topics.definition: A system call is the programming interface to the kernel and system programs are utilities built on those calls.

children.title: How a system call works
children.definition: A trap switches the CPU to kernel mode, the service routine runs and control returns with a result.

children.title: Types of system calls
children.definition: Process control, file management, device management, information maintenance, communication and protection.

children.title: System programs
children.definition: Compilers, editors, shells, utilities and command interpreters that users run directly.

children.title: Kernel mode and user mode
children.definition: Privileged instructions run only in kernel mode, which protects the system from user programs.

children.title: Operating system design goals
children.definition: Efficiency, reliability, maintainability and a clear interface between mechanism and policy.

card.explanation: A system call is the doorway through which a program asks the kernel to do something for it. The call traps, which switches the processor to kernel mode, the service routine runs, and control returns with a result. Calls fall into groups: process control, file management, device management, information maintenance, communication and protection. Privileged instructions may run only in kernel mode, which is what keeps a user program from damaging the system. System programs such as compilers, editors and shells sit above the calls, and the design goal is to separate mechanism from policy.
card.example: A program calling open on a file does not read the disk itself. It traps into the kernel, which checks the permission and returns a file descriptor.

quiz.q: What switches the processor from user mode to kernel mode?
options: A function call inside the program
quiz.why: The trap raises the privilege level so the kernel routine can run safely.

quiz.q: Why are privileged instructions restricted to kernel mode?
options: They could change the state of the whole machine
quiz.why: Instructions that touch the hardware or the memory map must not be reachable by user code.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a category of system calls?
quiz.why: The categories are process control, file, device, information, communication and protection.

quiz.q: Which is a system program rather than a system call?
quiz.why: A shell is a program built on top of the calls, while fork, open and read are calls themselves.

quiz.q: What does separating mechanism from policy mean?
options: Providing the tool in the kernel but leaving the decision to higher levels
quiz.why: The kernel supplies how something can be done, and policy decides when it should be done.

card.examTip: Describe the trap sequence in three steps, list the call categories, and state the kernel and user mode rule.

topics.title: Processes and Process Scheduling
topics.definition: A process is a program in execution with its own state, and the scheduler decides which process runs on the CPU.

children.title: Process concept and program versus process
children.definition: The program is passive code while the process is the active execution with a program counter and data.

children.title: Process control block (PCB)
children.definition: Stores process id, state, program counter, registers, memory limits, open files and accounting information.

children.title: Process states
children.definition: New, ready, running, waiting and terminated, with transitions triggered by scheduler decisions and events.

children.title: Scheduling queues and schedulers
children.definition: Job queue, ready queue and device queues served by long term, short term and medium term schedulers.

children.title: Context switch
children.definition: Saving the state of the running process and loading another, which is pure overhead.

children.title: Operations on processes
children.definition: Creation with fork, execution with exec, termination, and waiting by the parent with wait.

children.title: Co-operating processes and interprocess communication
children.definition: Independent processes do not affect each other while co-operating ones share data through shared memory or message passing, including pipes and sockets.

card.explanation: A program is passive code on disk, while a process is that program in execution with a program counter and data. Everything the kernel knows about a process is kept in its process control block. That holds the identifier, the state, the registers, the memory limits and the open files. A process moves through the states new, ready, running, waiting and terminated. Queues hold the processes at each stage, and the long term, short term and medium term schedulers move them along. Switching from one running process to another is a context switch, which does no useful work.
card.example: Opening a browser and a text editor gives two processes. The kernel keeps a control block for each and swaps between them, saving the registers of one and loading the other.

quiz.q: What is the difference between a program and a process?
options: A program is passive code, a process is that code in execution
A process is stored on disk
A program has a program counter
quiz.why: Only the running instance has a program counter, registers and a current state.

quiz.q: What does the process control block hold?
options: State, program counter, registers, memory limits and open files
quiz.why: It is the complete description the kernel needs to stop and restart the process.

quiz.q: Which statement about processes is NOT correct?
options: A context switch saves and restores process state
The short term scheduler picks the next process to run
A context switch does useful work for the user
Processes may be new, ready, running, waiting or terminated
quiz.why: A context switch is pure overhead, because no application work happens while it runs.

quiz.q: Which scheduler decides which process is admitted to memory first?
quiz.why: The long term scheduler controls the degree of multiprogramming by admitting jobs.

quiz.q: Which mechanism lets two processes exchange data through the kernel?
quiz.why: Shared memory and message passing, including pipes and sockets, are the two classic ways.

card.examTip: Draw the five state diagram with the transition labels, then list what the process control block stores.

topics.title: CPU Scheduling
topics.definition: CPU scheduling decides the order in which ready processes get the processor, which decides throughput and response time.

children.title: Scheduling criteria
children.definition: CPU utilisation, throughput, turnaround time, waiting time and response time.

children.title: First Come First Served (FCFS)
children.definition: Processes run in arrival order; simple but suffers the convoy effect with long jobs first.

children.title: Shortest Job First (SJF)
children.definition: Runs the process with the smallest next CPU burst, which is optimal for average waiting time but needs burst prediction.

children.title: Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF)
children.definition: The preemptive version of SJF, in which a newly arrived shorter job takes over the CPU.

children.title: Priority scheduling
children.definition: The highest priority process runs, with the risk of starvation, which ageing can prevent.

children.title: Round Robin (RR)
children.definition: Each process gets a fixed time quantum in rotation, which suits time sharing; the quantum size decides the overhead.

children.title: Multilevel queue and multilevel feedback queue
children.definition: Separate queues for different classes of jobs and migration between queues to balance responsiveness and throughput.

children.title: Multiple processor scheduling
children.definition: Load sharing, processor affinity and symmetric multiprocessing decide how threads are spread over CPUs.

card.explanation: Scheduling is judged on utilisation, throughput, turnaround time, waiting time and response time. First come first served runs jobs in arrival order, which is fair but lets one long job hold up the rest, the convoy effect. Shortest job first picks the smallest burst and gives the lowest average waiting time, but the burst length has to be predicted. Round robin gives each process a quantum in turn, which suits time sharing and makes the quantum size matter. Priority scheduling risks starvation, which ageing prevents, and multilevel feedback queues move jobs between queues.
card.example: With a quantum of 20 ms, five processes each get a turn within 100 ms, which feels instant to a user. With a quantum of 1 ms, most of the time goes into switching instead of working.

quiz.q: Which scheduling algorithm gives the lowest average waiting time?
quiz.why: Running the shortest burst first is provably optimal for average waiting time.

quiz.q: What problem does a long job at the front of the queue cause in FCFS?
quiz.why: Short jobs queue behind one long job, so all their waiting times rise together.

quiz.q: Which statement about scheduling is NOT correct?
options: Round robin gives each process a time quantum
SJF needs the burst length to be known or predicted
A very small quantum increases context switch overhead
quiz.why: A low priority process can wait indefinitely, which is why ageing raises its priority over time.

quiz.q: What does a multilevel feedback queue allow?
options: A job to move between queues based on its behaviour
quiz.why: Jobs that use up their whole quantum drop to a lower queue, which favours interactive work.

quiz.q: Which is the preemptive version of shortest job first?
quiz.why: Shortest remaining time first takes the processor away when a shorter job arrives.

card.examTip: Write the five criteria, then give each algorithm in one line with its advantage and its weakness.

topics.title: Critical Section Problem
topics.definition: The critical section problem is ensuring that processes update shared data one at a time while still making progress.

children.title: Critical section and race condition
children.definition: The critical section is the code that touches shared data, and a race condition is the wrong result caused by unsynchronised access.

children.title: Three requirements of a solution
children.definition: Mutual exclusion, progress and bounded waiting.

children.title: Peterson solution
children.definition: A two process software solution using a turn variable and a flag array.

children.title: Hardware support
children.definition: Disabling interrupts, test and set, and compare and swap instructions provide atomic primitives.

card.explanation: When two processes share data, the part of each that touches that data is its critical section. If both run at once the result depends on the timing, which is a race condition. A correct solution must guarantee three things. Mutual exclusion means only one process is inside at a time, and progress means the system is not stuck. Bounded waiting puts a limit on how long a process may wait to enter. Peterson's solution meets all three for two processes using a flag array and a turn variable. Hardware helps with atomic instructions such as test and set and compare and swap.
card.example: Two processes both add one to a shared counter. The result can be one less than it should be, because both read the old value before either writes the new one.

quiz.q: What is a race condition?
options: Two processes finishing at the same time
A result that depends on the timing of unsynchronised access to shared data
A process that never gets the CPU
quiz.why: The outcome changes with the interleaving, which is exactly what synchronisation removes.

quiz.q: Which is NOT one of the three requirements of a solution?
quiz.why: The three are mutual exclusion, progress and bounded waiting; preemption is a different idea.

quiz.q: Which statement about the critical section problem is NOT correct?
options: Disabling interrupts is a safe solution on a multiprocessor
The critical section is the code that touches shared data
Mutual exclusion allows one process at a time
quiz.why: Disabling interrupts stops only the local processor, so it fails when several share memory.

quiz.q: Which hardware instruction tests a value and sets it in one atomic step?
quiz.why: Test and set is the classic atomic primitive, and compare and swap is the other.

quiz.q: What does bounded waiting guarantee?
options: There is a limit on how long a process waits to enter the section
quiz.why: It stops a process being overtaken forever by others, which is what starvation means.

card.examTip: State the three requirements in one line each, then give Peterson's solution or a hardware primitive as the example.

topics.title: Semaphores
topics.definition: A semaphore is an integer variable accessed only through atomic wait and signal operations, used to control access to shared resources.

children.title: wait and signal operations
children.definition: wait decrements the value and blocks if it becomes negative; signal increments it and wakes a waiting process.

children.title: Binary and counting semaphores
children.definition: Binary semaphores take values 0 and 1 like a lock, while counting semaphores track a pool of resources.

children.title: Semaphore implementation and busy waiting
children.definition: Blocking implementations use queues instead of spinning, which avoids wasting CPU time.

children.title: Deadlock and starvation with semaphores
children.definition: Wrong ordering of waits can deadlock, and unfair scheduling can starve a process.

card.explanation: A semaphore is an integer that may only be changed through two atomic operations, wait and signal. Wait decrements the value and blocks the process if the result would be negative, and signal increments it and wakes one waiting process. A binary semaphore takes only zero and one, so it works as a lock. A counting semaphore tracks how many units of a resource are free. The first implementations used busy waiting, so blocking implementations put waiting processes in a queue instead. Used wrongly they still cause trouble: waits in the wrong order deadlock, and an unfair wake policy starves.
card.example: A printing pool with three printers is a counting semaphore starting at 3. Each job waits before printing and signals when it finishes, so the fourth job waits its turn.

quiz.q: What does the wait operation do?
options: Decrements the value and blocks if it would go negative
quiz.why: Wait is the request side of the pair, and it blocks when the resource is not available.

quiz.q: What is a binary semaphore used as?
quiz.why: Two values are enough to say locked or unlocked, which is what mutual exclusion needs.

quiz.q: Which statement about semaphores is NOT correct?
options: Semaphores remove the possibility of deadlock entirely
wait and signal must be atomic
A counting semaphore tracks a pool of resources
quiz.why: Two processes waiting on each other's semaphore still deadlock, so the ordering must be right.

quiz.q: Why is a blocking semaphore better than a busy waiting one?
options: Waiting processes use no processor time
quiz.why: A blocked process is put in a queue and woken later, instead of spinning in a loop.

quiz.q: A semaphore starts at 3. After five waits and two signals, what is its value?
quiz.why: Three minus five plus two gives zero, and two processes are blocked waiting.

card.examTip: Write wait and signal in pseudo code, then give one binary and one counting example.

topics.title: Classical Problems of Synchronisation
topics.definition: Three classic problems model the standard patterns of producer consumer, reader writer and multiple resource competition.

children.title: Producer consumer (bounded buffer)
children.definition: Producers wait when the buffer is full and consumers wait when it is empty, using empty, full and mutex semaphores.

children.title: Readers writers problem
children.definition: Several readers may read at once but a writer needs exclusive access; variants favour readers or writers.

children.title: Dining philosophers problem
children.definition: Five philosophers with five forks show deadlock and starvation; solutions include asymmetry and a waiter.

children.title: Sleeping barber and other models
children.definition: Further classical models used to study waiting, blocking and fairness.

card.explanation: Three problems are used to test any synchronisation tool. In the bounded buffer problem producers wait when the buffer is full and consumers when it is empty. Three semaphores do the work: empty, full and mutex. In the readers writers problem many readers may share the data, but a writer needs it alone; a solution either favours readers or writers. In the dining philosophers problem five philosophers share five forks, and taking one fork each deadlocks everyone. The fixes are asymmetry, a limit on how many may sit, or a waiter who grants permission.
card.example: A canteen counter is a bounded buffer: the cooks stop when the tray rack is full and the students wait when it is empty. The rack itself needs a mutex so two hands do not take the same tray.

quiz.q: In the bounded buffer problem, which semaphore makes a producer wait?
quiz.why: The producer waits on empty, because there is no slot left to put a new item into.

quiz.q: What happens if every philosopher picks up the left fork at once?
options: Deadlock, because each waits for the right fork
quiz.why: Each holds one resource and waits for another, which is the circular wait condition.

quiz.q: Which statement about the classical problems is NOT correct?
options: Several readers may read at the same time
The bounded buffer uses empty, full and mutex semaphores
The dining philosophers problem has no workable solution
A writer needs exclusive access to the shared data
quiz.why: Several solutions exist, including asymmetry, limiting the number at the table and a waiter.

quiz.q: What does the mutex semaphore protect in the bounded buffer?
options: The buffer itself, so only one process touches it at a time
quiz.why: Empty and full count the slots, while mutex guards the shared structure itself.

quiz.q: Which variant of the readers writers problem can starve a writer?
quiz.why: If readers keep arriving, a waiting writer may never get exclusive access.

card.examTip: Give the semaphore solution to the bounded buffer, then state the deadlock in dining philosophers and two fixes.

topics.title: Critical Regions and Monitors
topics.definition: Higher level constructs such as critical regions and monitors group synchronisation with the data they protect.

children.title: Conditional critical regions
children.definition: A region declares the shared variable and its condition, letting the language handle mutual exclusion.

children.title: Monitor concept
children.definition: A module holding shared data and procedures with automatic mutual exclusion, plus condition variables wait and signal.

children.title: Monitor solutions
children.definition: The producer consumer and dining philosophers problems are solved more cleanly with monitors than with raw semaphores.

children.title: Message passing as synchronisation
children.definition: Processes synchronise by exchanging messages with send and receive primitives instead of sharing memory.

card.explanation: Semaphores are flexible but easy to get wrong, so languages offer higher level tools. A conditional critical region declares the shared variable and the condition under which it may be touched, and the compiler adds the mutual exclusion. A monitor goes further. It is a module holding shared data and the procedures that work on it. Only one process may be inside at a time. Condition variables inside a monitor give the wait and signal operations, so a process can wait for a condition without holding the lock. Message passing is the alternative for systems without shared memory.
card.example: A monitor for a bank account holds the balance and the deposit and withdraw procedures. Only one caller can be inside either procedure, so the balance is never read half updated.

quiz.q: What does a monitor guarantee automatically?
options: Mutual exclusion, because only one process may be inside at a time
quiz.why: The compiler or runtime enforces the single entry rule, so the programmer cannot forget it.

quiz.q: What are condition variables used for inside a monitor?
options: Waiting for a condition without holding the lock
quiz.why: Wait releases the monitor so another process can enter, and signal wakes a waiter later.

quiz.q: Which statement about monitors is NOT correct?
options: A monitor holds shared data and its procedures
Only one process may be active inside a monitor
Condition variables provide wait and signal
Monitors remove the need to think about synchronisation at all
quiz.why: The exclusion is automatic, but which conditions to wait on is still the programmer's job.

quiz.q: When is message passing preferred over shared memory?
options: When processes run on different machines with no shared memory
When there is only one process
quiz.why: Without shared memory, sending a message through the kernel or the network is the only option.

quiz.q: What does a conditional critical region add to a plain critical region?
options: A condition that must hold before the region may be entered
quiz.why: The process waits until the condition is true, which is what the bounded buffer needs.

card.examTip: Contrast semaphores and monitors in two lines, then give wait and signal on a condition variable.

topics.title: Deadlocks
topics.definition: A deadlock is a set of processes each waiting for a resource held by another, so none can proceed.

children.title: Deadlock characterisation and four necessary conditions
children.definition: Mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption and circular wait must all hold.

children.title: Resource allocation graph
children.definition: Processes and resources as nodes with request, assignment and claim edges; a cycle suggests deadlock.

children.title: Deadlock prevention
children.definition: Break one necessary condition: request all resources at once, allow preemption, or impose an ordering on resources.

children.title: Deadlock avoidance and safe state
children.definition: The system refuses an allocation that would leave an unsafe state; the Banker algorithm tests safety.

children.title: Deadlock detection
children.definition: Use a wait-for graph or a reduction algorithm to find existing deadlocks.

children.title: Deadlock recovery
children.definition: Kill processes, preempt resources or roll back to a checkpoint.

children.title: Ignoring deadlocks
children.definition: Some systems assume deadlocks are rare and handle them manually, as UNIX often does.

card.explanation: A deadlock needs four conditions at once: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption and circular wait. Break any one of them and deadlock cannot occur, which is the prevention approach. A resource allocation graph draws processes and resources as nodes, and a cycle in the graph means deadlock is possible. Avoidance refuses an allocation that would leave the system in an unsafe state, and the Banker's algorithm is the standard test for that. Detection lets deadlocks happen, finds them with a wait for graph, then recovers by aborting a process or taking a resource back.
card.example: Two processes each hold a printer and ask for the scanner the other holds. The resource allocation graph has a cycle, and neither process can finish.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT a necessary condition for deadlock?
quiz.why: The condition is no preemption, so allowing resources to be taken away is a prevention method.

quiz.q: What does the Banker's algorithm test?
options: Whether a deadlock has already happened
Whether granting a request leaves the system in a safe state
quiz.why: A safe state is one in which some order lets every process still finish.

quiz.q: Which statement about deadlocks is NOT correct?
options: Detection is impossible once a deadlock has occurred
A cycle in the resource allocation graph signals possible deadlock
Prevention breaks one of the four conditions
Imposing a resource ordering prevents circular wait
quiz.why: Detection works with a wait for graph, and recovery then aborts or preempts to break it.

quiz.q: How can circular wait be prevented?
options: By imposing a total ordering on resource types
quiz.why: If every process asks in the same order, no cycle can form in the graph.

quiz.q: What is a safe state?
options: One in which no process is running
One in which some sequence lets every process finish
quiz.why: Safety is about the existence of a completion order, which is what the Banker's algorithm checks.

card.examTip: List the four conditions, then give one handling method for each: prevention, avoidance, detection and recovery.

topics.title: Threads and Multithreading Models
topics.definition: A thread is a lightweight unit of execution within a process, sharing memory with other threads of the same process.

children.title: Thread concept and thread control block
children.definition: A thread has its own program counter, registers and stack, but shares code, data and open files.

children.title: Benefits of threads
children.definition: Responsiveness, resource sharing, economy and better use of multiprocessor systems.

children.title: User level versus kernel level threads
children.definition: User threads are managed in a library without kernel help, while kernel threads are scheduled by the operating system.

children.title: Many to one model
children.definition: Many user threads map to one kernel thread, which is fast but one blocking call blocks all.

children.title: One to one model
children.definition: Each user thread has a kernel thread, giving true concurrency at the cost of overhead.

children.title: Many to many model
children.definition: Many user threads share a smaller number of kernel threads, combining the benefits of both.

children.title: Multithreading in practice
children.definition: Thread libraries such as POSIX threads, Java threads and threading models of Windows and Linux.

card.explanation: A thread is a unit of execution inside a process, lighter to create and switch than a whole process. Each thread keeps its own program counter, registers and stack, but shares the code, the data and the open files with its siblings. Threads make an application responsive, because one can keep the interface alive while another does the work. User level threads are managed by a library with no kernel involvement, while kernel level threads are scheduled by the operating system. The three mapping models are many to one, one to one and many to many.
card.example: A word processor keeps one thread for typing, one for spell checking and one for autosave. All three share the same document in memory, which is why threads cost less than separate processes.

quiz.q: What does a thread NOT share with its sibling threads?
quiz.why: Each thread needs its own execution state, while code, data and files are shared.

quiz.q: Which model maps many user threads onto one kernel thread?
quiz.why: It is fast, but one blocking system call stops every thread in the process.

quiz.q: Which statement about threads is NOT correct?
options: The one to one model gives true concurrency on several processors
User level threads are scheduled directly by the kernel
Threads share memory within a process
Creating a thread costs less than creating a process
quiz.why: User threads are managed by a library in user space, so the kernel cannot schedule them individually.

quiz.q: Why is the one to one model more expensive?
options: It uses more memory for registers
Each user thread needs its own kernel thread, which costs overhead
quiz.why: Every thread becomes a kernel object, so creating and switching them costs more.

quiz.q: Which benefit comes from giving the user interface its own thread?
options: Responsiveness, because the interface keeps working during a long task
quiz.why: A blocking task on another thread leaves the interface thread free to answer clicks.

card.examTip: Draw the three mapping models, then write two lines on user threads versus kernel threads.

topics.title: Memory Management Basics
topics.definition: Memory management keeps track of every byte of memory and decides which processes get it and when.

children.title: Address binding and its stages
children.definition: Instructions and data are bound to addresses at compile time, load time or execution time.

children.title: Logical and physical address space
children.definition: The logical address is generated by the CPU and the physical address is the one the memory unit sees, related by the memory management unit.

children.title: Memory management unit and relocation register
children.definition: Hardware that adds a base value to every logical address to produce the physical address.

children.title: Dynamic loading and linking
children.definition: Routines are loaded or linked only when needed, which saves memory and improves start up time.

children.title: Overlays and protection
children.definition: Overlays keep only needed sections of a large program in memory, while base and limit registers protect processes from each other.

card.explanation: Memory management tracks who is using which bytes and hands memory out as processes need it. An address can be bound at compile time, at load time or during execution, and the later the binding, the more flexible the system. The CPU generates logical addresses, and the memory unit sees physical ones; the memory management unit converts one into the other. Typically it adds a base value from a relocation register to each logical address. Base and limit registers also protect processes from one another, and dynamic loading and linking bring in code only when it is needed.
card.example: A program compiled to start at address 0 can run anywhere in memory. The relocation register holds the real starting address, and every logical address is adjusted by it.

quiz.q: What converts a logical address into a physical address?
quiz.why: The MMU sits between the CPU and memory and translates on every reference.

quiz.q: Which binding time gives the most flexibility?
quiz.why: Binding during execution lets a process be moved in memory while it runs.

quiz.q: Which statement about memory management is NOT correct?
options: A physical address is what the memory unit sees
Base and limit registers give protection
Dynamic linking loads the whole program before it starts
A logical address is generated by the CPU
quiz.why: Dynamic linking defers the linking until the routine is called, which saves memory.

quiz.q: What do base and limit registers do?
options: Define the legal address range of a process
quiz.why: Any address outside the range causes a trap, stopping one process reaching another's memory.

quiz.q: What problem do overlays solve?
options: Running a program larger than the memory available
quiz.why: Only the needed sections are kept in memory, and the rest are brought in over them.

card.examTip: Draw the CPU, MMU and memory with the logical and physical addresses labelled, then list the three binding times.

topics.title: Contiguous Memory Allocation and Swapping
topics.definition: In contiguous allocation each process occupies one continuous block of memory, and swapping moves whole processes to disk and back.

children.title: Fixed and variable partitioning
children.definition: Fixed partitions have set sizes while variable partitions are created on demand to fit each process.

children.title: First fit, best fit and worst fit
children.definition: Allocation strategies that choose the first, the tightest or the largest suitable hole in the free list.

children.title: Internal and external fragmentation
children.definition: Internal fragmentation wastes space inside an allocated block while external fragmentation leaves many small unusable holes.

children.title: Compaction
children.definition: Shifting processes together to merge holes, which costs time and is possible only with relocatable code.

children.title: Swapping and the backing store
children.definition: A whole process moves to disk and back, which is slow but frees memory for others.

card.explanation: In contiguous allocation each process sits in one unbroken block of memory. Fixed partitioning cuts memory into set sizes, which wastes space inside a partition. Variable partitioning creates a hole sized for each process as it arrives. Placing a process means choosing a hole: first fit takes the first one big enough, best fit the tightest, and worst fit the largest. Over time small unusable holes appear, which is external fragmentation. Compaction pushes the processes together to merge the holes, and swapping moves a whole process out to disk to free memory.
card.example: A 20 KB process in a 24 KB fixed partition wastes 4 KB, which is internal fragmentation. Several small free holes that no job fits into are external fragmentation.

quiz.q: Which placement strategy picks the smallest hole that is still big enough?
quiz.why: Best fit leaves the smallest leftover, though it tends to create many tiny holes.

quiz.q: What is internal fragmentation?
options: A page table that is too large
Wasted space inside an allocated block
quiz.why: The process did not need all of the block it was given, and the rest cannot be used.

quiz.q: Which statement about allocation is NOT correct?
options: First fit takes the first suitable hole
External fragmentation leaves unusable gaps between processes
Swapping moves a single page to disk
quiz.why: Swapping moves a whole process, while paging is the scheme that moves single pages.

quiz.q: What is the drawback of compaction?
options: It costs time and needs relocatable code
quiz.why: Moving processes while they run is expensive, and any absolute addresses must be adjustable.

quiz.q: What is the backing store used for?
options: Holding whole processes swapped out to disk
quiz.why: A swapped process waits on the backing store until memory frees up again.

card.examTip: Contrast internal and external fragmentation with an example of each, then give the three fit strategies.

topics.title: Paging
topics.definition: Paging divides physical memory into fixed size frames and logical memory into pages of the same size, removing external fragmentation.

children.title: Pages, frames and page table
children.definition: Each process keeps a page table mapping page numbers to frame numbers.

children.title: Address translation
children.definition: The logical address splits into a page number and an offset; the page table gives the frame and the offset locates the byte.

children.title: Translation lookaside buffer (TLB)
children.definition: A small associative cache of recent translations that avoids a memory lookup for every reference.

children.title: Effective access time
children.definition: The average access time combining the TLB hit ratio with the page table access time.

children.title: Shared pages and protection
children.definition: Read only pages such as library code can be shared by many processes with protection bits in the page table.

children.title: Multilevel and inverted page tables
children.definition: Hierarchical tables handle large address spaces while an inverted table keeps one entry per frame.

card.explanation: Paging cuts physical memory into frames and logical memory into pages of the same size, so a process need not be stored contiguously. Each process keeps a page table that maps each page number to a frame number. A logical address splits into a page number and an offset; the table gives the frame and the offset locates the byte. Looking the table up on every reference would be slow, so a translation lookaside buffer caches recent translations. Protection and sharing bits sit in the table, and large address spaces use multilevel or inverted tables.
card.example: With 4 KB pages, the logical address 8196 lies in page 2 at offset 4. If the page table puts page 2 in frame 7, the physical address is 7 times 4096 plus 4.

quiz.q: What does a page table hold?
options: The mapping from page number to frame number
quiz.why: There is one entry per page, and the entry names the frame holding that page.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of the translation lookaside buffer?
options: To cache recent address translations so lookups are fast
quiz.why: A TLB hit skips the extra memory read that a page table lookup would cost.

quiz.q: Which statement about paging is NOT correct?
options: Protection bits live in the page table
Pages and frames are the same size
quiz.why: A TLB speeds translation up, because most references hit in the cache.

quiz.q: With 4 KB pages, how many bits of the address are needed for the offset?
quiz.why: 4 KB is 2 to the power 12 bytes, so 12 bits locate the byte inside the page.

quiz.q: What is an inverted page table?
options: A table with one entry per process
A table with one entry per physical frame
quiz.why: It scales with memory size rather than process count, which saves space.

card.examTip: Draw the translation from logical to physical address, then state the TLB hit ratio effect on access time.

topics.title: Segmentation
topics.definition: Segmentation divides a program into logical units such as code, stack and data, each with its own base and limit.

children.title: Segments and segment table
children.definition: Each segment has a name, a length and a base address held in the segment table.

children.title: Address translation in segmentation
children.definition: The segment number selects the entry and the offset must be within the segment limit.

children.title: Segmentation with paging
children.definition: Segments are paged to remove external fragmentation while keeping the logical structure.

children.title: Paging versus segmentation
children.definition: Paging is invisible to the programmer and fixed size, segmentation reflects program structure and is variable size.

card.explanation: Segmentation splits a program into units the programmer recognises: code, data, stack and so on. Each segment has a name, a length and a base address, all held in the segment table. An address is given as a segment number and an offset, and the hardware checks that the offset is inside the segment limit. Because segments vary in size, memory develops external fragmentation again. Combining the two schemes avoids that: each segment is paged, which keeps the logical structure and removes the fragmentation.
card.example: A program has a code segment, a data segment and a stack segment. The hardware refuses any access past the end of a segment, which catches an out of range array index at once.

quiz.q: What does each entry in a segment table hold?
options: A base address and a limit
quiz.why: The base says where the segment starts, and the limit says how far it reaches.

quiz.q: Why is segmentation visible to the programmer while paging is not?
options: Segments match the logical structure of the program
quiz.why: Code, data and stack are named units in the program, while pages are an invisible mechanism.

quiz.q: Which statement about segmentation is NOT correct?
options: The offset is checked against the segment limit
quiz.why: Variable sized segments leave holes, which is why segmentation is often combined with paging.

quiz.q: What does segmentation with paging combine?
options: The logical structure of segments with the fixed size of pages
quiz.why: The segment table points at a page table, so the structure survives and the holes do not.

quiz.q: If the offset in an address is larger than the segment limit, what happens?
options: A trap is raised for an addressing error
quiz.why: The limit check is a hardware protection, and it catches out of range accesses at once.

card.examTip: Draw the segment table translation, then write a two line comparison of paging and segmentation.

topics.title: Virtual Memory and Demand Paging
topics.definition: Virtual memory lets a process run even when only part of it is in memory, by loading pages on demand and keeping the rest on disk.

children.title: Virtual memory concept and benefits
children.definition: Programs larger than physical memory can run, more processes fit in memory and loading is faster.

children.title: Demand paging and the valid-invalid bit
children.definition: A page is brought in only when referenced; the valid bit marks which pages are actually in memory.

children.title: Page fault handling
children.definition: The trap finds the page on disk, finds a free frame, reads the page, updates the table and restarts the instruction.

children.title: Copy on write
children.definition: Parent and child share pages until one of them writes, which makes process creation cheap.

children.title: Effective access time with page faults
children.definition: The very high cost of a fault dominates the average access time, so fault rates must stay low.

card.explanation: Virtual memory lets a program run when only part of it is in memory, and it makes a program larger than physical memory possible. Under demand paging a page is brought in only when it is referenced, and the valid invalid bit records which pages are really present. A reference to a missing page causes a page fault. The operating system finds the page on disk, gets a free frame and reads it in. It then updates the table and restarts the instruction. A fault costs so much that even a small fault rate ruins performance.
card.example: Opening a large application starts at once, because only the first few pages are loaded. The rest arrive as the user reaches the features that need them.

quiz.q: What marks whether a page is currently in memory?
quiz.why: A valid entry means the page is resident; an invalid one means a reference will fault.

quiz.q: What is the last step of handling a page fault?
options: Restarting the instruction that caused the fault
quiz.why: The instruction could not complete, so it runs again once the page is in place.

quiz.q: Which statement about virtual memory is NOT correct?
options: Pages are loaded only when referenced
More processes can fit in memory at once
Virtual memory removes the need for a disk
A program larger than physical memory can run
quiz.why: The disk holds the pages that are not resident, so it is essential to the scheme.

quiz.q: What does copy on write do?
options: Writes every page to disk at once
Copies the whole process on every fork
Shares pages until one side writes, then copies that page
quiz.why: Most pages are never written after a fork, so deferring the copy saves time and memory.

quiz.q: Why must the page fault rate stay very low?
options: A fault costs thousands of times a normal memory access
The process ends after a few faults
quiz.why: Servicing a fault means disk I/O, so even one fault in ten thousand references hurts throughput.

card.examTip: List the steps of page fault handling in order, then note why the fault rate dominates access time.

topics.title: Page Replacement
topics.definition: Page replacement decides which page to remove from memory when a needed page must be brought in.

children.title: FIFO page replacement
children.definition: Replaces the oldest page, which is simple but can suffer Belady anomaly where more frames cause more faults.

children.title: Optimal page replacement
children.definition: Replaces the page used farthest in the future, giving the lowest fault rate but requiring future knowledge.

children.title: LRU page replacement
children.definition: Replaces the least recently used page, which approximates optimal behaviour and needs stack or counter hardware support.

children.title: LRU approximations: reference bit and clock
children.definition: The reference bit, additional reference bits and the second chance or clock algorithm approximate LRU cheaply.

children.title: Counting and stack algorithms
children.definition: LFU and MFU algorithms count references; stack algorithms such as LRU do not suffer Belady anomaly.

children.title: Frame allocation policies
children.definition: Equal, proportional and priority based allocation of frames among processes.

card.explanation: When memory is full and a page must come in, the system has to choose a victim. FIFO replaces the oldest page, which is simple but can show Belady's anomaly, where giving a process more frames actually raises the fault count. The optimal algorithm replaces the page used farthest in the future. It gives the lowest possible fault rate, but it cannot be implemented. LRU replaces the least recently used page and approximates the optimal well. Cheaper approximations use a reference bit and the clock or second chance algorithm, and stack algorithms such as LRU never show Belady's anomaly.
card.example: With the reference string 1, 2, 3, 1, 2 and three frames, no replacement is needed. With two frames the system must evict one, and how it chooses decides the fault count.

quiz.q: Which algorithm gives the lowest possible page fault rate?
quiz.why: Knowing the future lets it pick the victim that will not be needed for longest.

quiz.q: What is Belady's anomaly?
options: A page that is never used
A frame that is always free
More frames causing more page faults
quiz.why: It is counter intuitive, and algorithms keeping a stack of pages such as LRU do not show it.

quiz.q: Which statement about replacement is NOT correct?
options: The clock algorithm approximates LRU cheaply
The optimal algorithm is used in most real systems
quiz.why: The future reference string is unknown at run time, so optimal is only a benchmark.

quiz.q: How does the second chance or clock algorithm work?
options: It gives a page with its reference bit set a second chance and clears the bit
It never replaces a dirty page
It always replaces the oldest page
quiz.why: The hand sweeps the frames, clearing bits and evicting the first page whose bit is clear.

quiz.q: Which counting algorithm replaces the page used least often?
quiz.why: LFU counts references and evicts the lowest count, while MFU argues the other way.

card.examTip: Work one reference string through FIFO, optimal and LRU with three frames, and compare the fault counts.

topics.title: Thrashing
topics.definition: Thrashing is the state in which a system spends more time paging than executing useful work.

children.title: Causes of thrashing
children.definition: Too many processes compete for too few frames, so each faults immediately after a page is replaced.

children.title: Working set model
children.definition: Tracks the pages used in the last delta references and gives each process enough frames for its working set.

children.title: Page fault frequency control
children.definition: Adds frames to a process with a high fault rate and removes frames from one with a very low rate.

children.title: Locality of reference
children.definition: Programs tend to reuse a small set of pages, which is why working set control works.

card.explanation: Thrashing is what happens when the system spends more time paging than doing real work. Too many processes compete for too few frames, so each one faults as soon as it starts. The faulting process is suspended while its page is fetched. Throughput collapses while the operator sees frantic disk activity. The working set model fixes this by tracking the pages a process used in a recent window. The process is given at least that many frames. Page fault frequency control does the same by watching each process's fault rate.
card.example: A machine with eight heavy programs open and too little memory grinds to a halt. The disk light stays on and nothing finishes, because every process waits for a page.

quiz.q: What causes thrashing?
options: A processor that is too slow
Too many processes competing for too few frames
A disk that is too fast
quiz.why: Each process lacks the frames it needs, so it faults constantly and spends its time waiting.

quiz.q: What is a working set?
options: All the pages of a process
The free frames in the system
The pages a process used in a recent window of references
quiz.why: It captures the pages a process is actively using, which is what must stay resident.

quiz.q: Which statement about thrashing is NOT correct?
options: Adding more processes is the usual cure
Throughput collapses while disk activity stays high
The working set model gives each process enough frames
Locality of reference is why working sets stay small
quiz.why: The cure is the opposite: suspend some processes so the rest get enough frames to work.

quiz.q: What does page fault frequency control do?
options: Adds frames to a process with a high fault rate and takes them from one with a low rate
Gives every process the same number of frames
quiz.why: The fault rate is the signal, and frames move to where they are doing the most good.

quiz.q: Why does the working set model work at all?
options: Because programs use only one page
Because memory is always large enough
quiz.why: Programs reuse a small set of pages for a while, so that set can be identified and kept.

card.examTip: Define thrashing, give its cause, then explain the working set model and the page fault frequency fix.

modules.title: Disk Scheduling, File Systems and Distributed File Systems

topics.title: Disk Structures and Disk Scheduling
topics.definition: A disk stores data on platters in tracks and sectors, and disk scheduling decides the order in which pending requests are served.

children.title: Disk structure
children.definition: Platters, surfaces, tracks, sectors and cylinders, with the head moving on an arm and the platter spinning.

children.title: Disk access time
children.definition: Seek time, rotational latency and transfer time together decide the cost of a request.

children.title: First Come First Served (FCFS)
children.definition: Requests are served in arrival order, which is fair but causes long head movement.

children.title: Shortest Seek Time First (SSTF)
children.definition: Serves the nearest request, which improves throughput but can starve far requests.

children.title: SCAN and C-SCAN
children.definition: The head sweeps back and forth like an elevator; C-SCAN returns to the start without serving on the return trip for uniform waiting.

children.title: LOOK and C-LOOK
children.definition: Like SCAN and C-SCAN but the head reverses at the last request instead of the disk edge.

children.title: Selecting a disk scheduling algorithm
children.definition: Choice depends on load, fairness requirements and whether seek time dominates.

card.explanation: A disk holds data on spinning platters divided into tracks, and each track into sectors. Reading a block costs three things: seek time to move the head, rotational latency to wait for the sector, and transfer time to read it. Seek time usually dominates, so the order requests are served in matters a great deal. First come first served is fair but lets the head wander. Shortest seek time first picks the nearest request, which is fast but can starve a far one. SCAN sweeps the head back and forth like an elevator, and C-SCAN returns without serving to even out the wait.
card.example: With requests at cylinders 98, 183, 37 and 122 starting from 53, FCFS moves the head a long way. SSTF would serve 37 first, cutting the total head movement sharply.

quiz.q: Which component of disk access time usually dominates?
quiz.why: Moving the arm mechanically is far slower than spinning or transferring, so seek decides the order.

quiz.q: How does C-SCAN differ from SCAN?
options: C-SCAN serves in one direction and returns without serving
C-SCAN only works on solid state drives
quiz.why: Serving in one direction only makes the waiting time more even for requests at the edges.

quiz.q: Which statement about disk scheduling is NOT correct?
options: LOOK reverses at the last request instead of the disk edge
FCFS gives the shortest total head movement
SCAN works like an elevator sweeping back and forth
SSTF can starve a request far from the head
quiz.why: FCFS is the fair but wasteful one; SSTF and SCAN cut head movement dramatically.

quiz.q: A disk queue has requests at 10, 90 and 30, and the head is at 50 moving upward. Which does SCAN serve first?
quiz.why: The head is moving up, so the next request above it, at 90, is served first.

quiz.q: What does LOOK do differently from SCAN?
options: It sorts by sector instead of cylinder
It reverses at the last request, not at the disk edge
quiz.why: Reversing at the last request saves the wasted sweep to the end of the disk.

card.examTip: List seek time, latency and transfer time, then work one queue through FCFS, SSTF and SCAN and compare movement.

topics.title: File System Interface
topics.definition: A file is a named collection of related information, and the file system interface defines how users and programs work with it.

children.title: File attributes and operations
children.definition: Name, identifier, type, location, size, protection, timestamps; operations include create, open, read, write, seek, delete and truncate.

children.title: File types and structure
children.definition: Text and binary files, executable files and directories, with internal structure from none to indexed.

children.title: Access methods
children.definition: Sequential access reads in order, direct or relative access jumps to a block and indexed access uses an index of keys.

children.title: Directory structures
children.definition: Single level, two level, tree, and acyclic graph directories with path names and current directory.

children.title: File sharing and protection
children.definition: Access rights, access control lists and permission bits decide who may read, write or execute.

card.explanation: A file is a named collection of information stored on secondary storage. It carries attributes such as a name, an identifier, a type, a location, a size, protection and timestamps. The operations a program can ask for are create, open, read, write, seek, delete and truncate. Data can be reached sequentially, directly by block number, or through an index of keys. Directories hold the names and let them be organised as a single level list, a two level list, a tree or an acyclic graph. Protection decides who may read, write or execute.
card.example: Reading a database table record by record is sequential access. Jumping straight to the row with a known key, as an index allows, is direct access.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a file operation?
quiz.why: The operations are create, open, read, write, seek, delete and truncate; routing is a network idea.

quiz.q: Which access method jumps straight to a record with a known key?
quiz.why: Indexed access keeps an index of keys pointing at blocks, which is how a database finds one row.

quiz.q: Which statement about directories is NOT correct?
options: An acyclic graph directory allows sharing
A two level directory gives every user the same directory
A single level directory holds all files in one list
quiz.why: Two level directories give each user their own directory, which is the point of the scheme.

quiz.q: Which file attribute records when the file was last changed?
quiz.why: Timestamps record creation, last modification and last access, which backup tools rely on.

quiz.q: What does the protection attribute control?
options: Who may read, write or execute the file
quiz.why: Access rights, permission bits and access control lists are all ways of expressing it.

card.examTip: List the seven attributes and the seven operations, then give the three access methods with an example each.

topics.title: File System Implementation
topics.definition: Implementation covers how files, directories and free space are actually stored on disk.

children.title: File system layers and structures
children.definition: Application, logical file system, file organisation module, basic file system, I/O control and devices.

children.title: On disk structures
children.definition: Boot control block, volume control block, directory structure and per file control block.

children.title: In memory structures
children.definition: Mount table, directory cache, system wide open file table and per process file table.

children.title: Mounting and partitions
children.definition: Volumes are mounted into the directory tree at a mount point, with optional virtual file system support.

children.title: Directory implementation
children.definition: A linear list of names and pointers or a hash table for faster lookup.

children.title: Allocation methods
children.definition: Contiguous allocation is fast but suffers fragmentation; linked allocation has no external fragmentation but slow random access; indexed allocation with index blocks supports direct access.

children.title: Free space management
children.definition: Bit vectors, linked lists, grouping and counting track which blocks are available.

children.title: Efficiency and performance
children.definition: Caching, buffering, read ahead and careful block size choice improve throughput.

card.explanation: On disk a file system needs a boot control block, a volume control block, the directory structure and a control block for each file. In memory it keeps a mount table, a directory cache, a system wide open file table and a per process table. Three allocation methods exist. Contiguous allocation is fast and simple but cannot grow and fragments the disk. Linked allocation removes external fragmentation but only supports slow sequential access. Indexed allocation keeps an index block of pointers, which supports direct access at the cost of the index.
card.example: Unix inodes are indexed allocation: one block holds the attributes and a list of pointers to the data blocks, with indirect blocks for large files.

quiz.q: Which allocation method suffers external fragmentation and cannot grow a file easily?
quiz.why: A file needs one unbroken run of blocks, so it cannot grow past its neighbours.

quiz.q: What does an inode hold?
options: The file attributes and the pointers to its data blocks
quiz.why: The name lives in the directory entry, which points at the inode holding everything else.

quiz.q: Which statement about implementation is NOT correct?
options: A bit vector is one way to track free space
A directory can be a linear list or a hash table
Linked allocation gives the fastest random access
quiz.why: Following a chain of pointers means sequential access only, which is its main weakness.

quiz.q: What is a mount table used for?
options: Recording which file systems are mounted where
quiz.why: It ties each mounted volume to its mount point in the directory tree.

quiz.q: Which method tracks free space with one bit per block?
quiz.why: A bit vector is compact and makes finding a run of free blocks easy.

card.examTip: Draw the on disk and in memory structures, then compare contiguous, linked and indexed allocation in a table.

topics.title: Distributed File Systems
topics.definition: A distributed file system lets users access files stored on remote machines as if they were local.

children.title: Naming and transparency
children.definition: Naming schemes map file names to locations; location transparency hides where the file is and location independence allows it to move.

children.title: Remote file access
children.definition: Remote service sends each request to the server while caching keeps copies locally; cache consistency must be managed.

children.title: Stateful versus stateless service
children.definition: A stateful server remembers client information between requests, which allows better performance but needs recovery; a stateless server treats each request independently.

children.title: File replication
children.definition: Copies of a file on several servers improve availability and performance but require update propagation.

children.title: Case study: NFS and AFS
children.definition: The network file system and the Andrew file system illustrate caching and session semantics.

card.explanation: A distributed file system makes files on other machines look local. Naming turns a name into a location. Location transparency hides where the file sits, and location independence lets it move without the name changing. Access is either remote service, where every request goes to the server, or caching, where a copy is held locally and consistency must be managed. A stateful server remembers clients between requests, which is faster but needs crash recovery. A stateless server keeps nothing, so a restart is cheap. Replication copies files for availability, at the price of update propagation.
card.example: A lab mounts the department file server over NFS, so every machine sees the same home directories. The server is stateless enough that a reboot loses no client state.

quiz.q: What does location transparency mean?
options: The user need not know where the file physically is
quiz.why: The name stays the same whatever machine the file is actually stored on.

quiz.q: Which statement about distributed file systems is NOT correct?
options: Caching keeps a local copy for speed
A stateless server keeps no client state between requests
A stateful server needs no crash recovery at all
quiz.why: Remembering client state is exactly what makes recovery necessary after a crash.

quiz.q: What is the main cost of file replication?
options: More disk space and the need to propagate updates
quiz.why: Every copy has to be kept in step, and that is the hard part of replication.

quiz.q: Which is a distributed file system named in the syllabus?
quiz.why: NFS, the network file system, and AFS, the Andrew file system, are the two case studies.

quiz.q: Why might a stateless design be preferred?
options: A server crash loses no client state, so recovery is simple
quiz.why: With nothing remembered, the server restarts and the clients carry on.

card.examTip: Define transparency, contrast stateful and stateless service, then name NFS and AFS with one line each.

modules.title: Case Studies: Linux, Windows, Android and Virtual Machines

topics.title: Linux System
topics.definition: Linux is a free, open source, monolithic but modular UNIX like kernel with strong process and file management.

children.title: Design principles
children.definition: Multiuser, multitasking, portable, modular and open source, with everything presented as a file.

children.title: Kernel structure and modules
children.definition: Loadable kernel modules extend the kernel at run time without reboot, and the shell is the user interface.

children.title: Process management in Linux
children.definition: fork and exec create processes, the scheduler uses a fair priority scheme, signals communicate with processes and process states resemble UNIX.

children.title: File systems in Linux
children.definition: The virtual file system layer supports ext4, XFS and others, with inodes, directories, links and mount points.

children.title: Memory and device management
children.definition: Virtual memory with demand paging and swap space, plus device drivers and special files.

children.title: Users, groups and permissions
children.definition: root and ordinary users, file permission bits and the sudo mechanism for privilege.

card.explanation: Linux is a free, open source, UNIX like kernel that is monolithic but modular. Loadable kernel modules let drivers be added while the system runs, so the kernel grows without a rebuild. Processes are created with fork and exec, and the scheduler uses a fair priority scheme. Its virtual file system layer supports many file systems such as ext4 and XFS through one interface, with inodes, directories, links and mount points underneath. Memory uses demand paging with swap space, and devices appear as special files. Users, groups and permission bits control access, with sudo for privilege.
card.example: A driver for a new webcam can be inserted while the machine runs, and removed again without a reboot. That is what loadable kernel modules make possible.

quiz.q: How does Linux create a new process?
quiz.why: Fork copies the process and exec replaces its program, which is the classic UNIX pair.

quiz.q: What does the virtual file system layer do?
options: Gives one interface over several different file systems
quiz.why: Programs use one set of calls whether the disk holds ext4, XFS or something else.

quiz.q: Which statement about Linux is NOT correct?
options: It uses demand paging with swap
It is a microkernel with everything running as a user process
Kernel modules can be loaded at run time
quiz.why: Linux is monolithic; it only borrows modular loading from microkernel designs.

quiz.q: What does sudo do?
options: Runs one command with root privilege
quiz.why: It grants a single command the rights of root without logging in as root.

quiz.q: Which file system is commonly used on Linux today?
quiz.why: ext4 is the standard Linux file system, and XFS and Btrfs are also supported.

card.examTip: Write the design principles, then one line each on processes, the VFS layer, memory and permissions.

topics.title: MS Windows System
topics.definition: Windows is a commercial, closed source operating system with a layered, object oriented environment and a hybrid kernel.

children.title: System structure
children.definition: Hardware abstraction layer, kernel, executive services, device drivers, subsystems and the user mode environment.

children.title: Objects, handles and registry
children.definition: Executive objects manipulated through handles, with the registry storing system configuration.

children.title: Process and thread management
children.definition: Processes as containers of threads, the dispatcher database, priority based preemptive scheduling and fibres.

children.title: Memory management in Windows
children.definition: Demand paging on a 64 bit address space with working set management and a page frame database.

children.title: File system and security
children.definition: NTFS with journaling, compression and encryption, and an access token based security model.

card.explanation: Windows is a commercial system built around a layered, object oriented design with a hybrid kernel. At the bottom sits a hardware abstraction layer, then the kernel, then executive services, then device drivers and subsystems, with the user environment on top. The executive works with objects, and programs reach them through handles rather than names. Configuration lives in the registry instead of in scattered text files. Processes are containers for threads, and the dispatcher schedules threads by priority with preemption. NTFS provides journaling, compression and encryption, and security uses access tokens.
card.example: A Windows program opens a file and receives a handle. Every later read and write passes that handle, so the object it points at can be renamed without breaking the program.

quiz.q: What does the hardware abstraction layer do?
options: Hides differences between hardware platforms from the kernel above
quiz.why: The rest of the system sees one machine, which is what makes Windows portable across hardware.

quiz.q: How do Windows programs refer to executive objects?
quiz.why: A handle is an indirect reference the kernel resolves, so objects can be moved or renamed.

quiz.q: Which statement about Windows is NOT correct?
options: Windows uses a pure microkernel with no kernel mode services
The scheduler works on threads, not processes
quiz.why: Windows has a hybrid kernel, with many services still running in kernel mode.

quiz.q: What is an access token used for?
options: Carrying the security identity and privileges of a user or process
quiz.why: Every process carries a token, and the system checks it against the object's access rules.

quiz.q: Which file system does Windows use by default today?
quiz.why: NTFS adds journaling, compression, encryption and access control to the older FAT designs.

card.examTip: Draw the layer stack from the hardware abstraction layer up, then add a line on handles, the registry and NTFS.

topics.title: Android OS
topics.definition: Android is a mobile operating system built on a modified Linux kernel with a Java like application framework.

children.title: Android architecture
children.definition: Layers are the Linux kernel, hardware abstraction layer, native libraries with ART, Android runtime, application framework and applications.

children.title: Application components
children.definition: Activity, Service, Broadcast Receiver and Content Provider are the building blocks of an Android app.

children.title: Activity and application life cycle
children.definition: onCreate, onStart, onResume, onPause, onStop, onRestart and onDestroy manage state and resources.

children.title: Dalvik and ART
children.definition: Dalvik used just in time compilation from DEX bytecode while ART uses ahead of time and profile guided compilation.

children.title: Security and permissions
children.definition: Each app runs in its own sandbox under a unique user id and requests permissions for sensitive operations.

card.explanation: Android is a mobile system built on a modified Linux kernel. Its layers are the kernel, a hardware abstraction layer, native libraries with the runtime, the application framework and the applications themselves. An app is built from four kinds of component: activities, services, broadcast receivers and content providers. An activity moves through a life cycle of callbacks: onCreate, onStart, onResume, onPause, onStop and onDestroy. That lets the system reclaim memory at any point. Old versions ran Dalvik, which compiled during execution, while ART compiles ahead of time.
card.example: Rotating the phone destroys and recreates the activity, so onCreate runs again. Saving state in onPause is what keeps the user's place from being lost.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT an Android application component?
quiz.why: The four components are Activity, Service, Broadcast Receiver and Content Provider.

quiz.q: What replaced Dalvik in later Android versions?
quiz.why: The Android runtime compiles applications ahead of time instead of during execution.

quiz.q: Which statement about Android is NOT correct?
options: It is built on a modified Linux kernel
Each app runs in its own sandbox with a unique user id
An activity has a life cycle the system controls
Apps share one user id so they can read each other's files freely
quiz.why: Each app gets its own id, which is what keeps one app out of another's data.

quiz.q: Which callback runs when the activity becomes visible and interactive?
quiz.why: onResume is where the activity is in the foreground and the user can interact with it.

quiz.q: How does an app get permission to use the camera?
options: It declares the permission and the user grants it at install or run time
quiz.why: Permissions are declared in the manifest and granted by the user, which is the sandbox model.

card.examTip: Draw the five layers of the stack, list the four components, and give the activity life cycle in order.

topics.title: Virtual Machine Operating Systems
topics.definition: A virtual machine presents a complete hardware-like environment in software so several operating systems can share one physical machine.

children.title: Virtual machine concept
children.definition: A layer of software creates an illusion of separate hardware for each guest operating system.

children.title: Type 1 and type 2 hypervisors
children.definition: Type 1 runs directly on hardware for servers, type 2 runs as an application on a host operating system.

children.title: CPU, memory and I/O virtualisation
children.definition: Privileged instructions are trapped or handled in hardware, memory is mapped with shadow or nested page tables, and devices are emulated or passed through.

children.title: Benefits of virtualisation
children.definition: Server consolidation, isolation, mobility of workloads, snapshots and easier testing.

children.title: Containers versus virtual machines
children.definition: Containers share the host kernel and isolate processes, which is lighter but less isolated than a full virtual machine.

card.explanation: A virtual machine is software that looks like a complete computer to the operating system running inside it. The layer that does this is called a hypervisor. A type 1 hypervisor runs directly on the hardware, which is what data centres use. A type 2 hypervisor runs as an application on a host operating system. Three things must be virtualised. The processor is handled by trapping privileged instructions, and memory by mapping guest addresses through shadow or nested page tables. Devices are emulated or passed through. Containers are the lighter alternative, sharing the host kernel.
card.example: One physical server can host ten virtual machines. Each runs its own operating system and believes it owns the whole machine.

quiz.q: Which type of hypervisor runs directly on the hardware?
quiz.why: A bare metal hypervisor sits on the hardware, and the guest systems run above it.

quiz.q: How is memory virtualised?
options: By mapping guest addresses through shadow or nested page tables
quiz.why: An extra level of address translation turns a guest physical address into a real one.

quiz.q: Which statement about virtualisation is NOT correct?
options: A virtual machine gives weaker isolation than a container
A type 2 hypervisor runs on a host operating system
Snapshots make testing and rollback easy
quiz.why: A virtual machine isolates at the hardware boundary, which is stronger than a shared kernel.

quiz.q: What happens when a guest runs a privileged instruction?
options: It is trapped and handled by the hypervisor
It always runs at full speed
quiz.why: Trapping is what lets the hypervisor keep control of the real hardware.

quiz.q: Why are containers lighter than virtual machines?
options: They share the host kernel and carry no full guest operating system
quiz.why: No full guest operating system means faster start up and far less overhead.

card.examTip: Contrast type 1 and type 2 hypervisors, name the three things virtualised, then compare containers with virtual machines.
